Title: Tata Mutual Fund launches Tata Quant Fund
Content:
~ A machine-driven mutual fund scheme that uses artificial intelligence to analyse prevailing market conditions and actively manage investment strategies ~ Highlights:
  • Open ended equity mutual fund scheme following quant-based investing theme
  • Medium to long term capital appreciation expected
  • The fund would invest in equity and equity related instruments which form part of S&P BSE 200 and Equity Derivative Segment
  • NFO opens on 03 January 2020 and closes on 17 January 2020
Mumbai, January 08, 2020: Tata Mutual Fund has launched 'Tata Quant Fund' an Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) powered fund. This fund employs a proprietary quant framework that combine multiple rule engines and predictive models to create investment portfolios that are aimed at maximizing returns during up-trending markets while minimizing losses during down trending phases. Broad and persistent factors of stock returns are used for building rule engines for portfolio creation. Each rule engine uses scoring to create concentrated portfolios with attributes like 'value', 'quality', 'momentum', 'size' and couple of combination attributes. Thereafter the ML powered predictive algorithms decide basis prevailing market and macro-economic conditions, portfolio with which attribute is likely to outperform during the next month. The algorithms also predict absolute direction (positive or negative) of return for the next month. Long position in selected portfolio is taken only for months where predicted return is positive. During months where predicted returns are negative, the strategy uses derivatives to hedge the gross long equity position held previously. Tata Quant Fund portfolios are rebalanced monthly for optimal performance at low risks. The predictive engines use more than past 20 years of market and macro-economic data to analyse hidden relationships and patterns. These correlations along with prevailing market and macro-economic data are then used by the engines for making monthly predictions. Thus, the investment decision making process of the fund is fully machine driven and free of human judgement. The machine learning predictive models also recalibrate and re-adjust at a fixed periodicity by using new and incremental data. This enables the models to factor in emerging patterns and relationships. These algorithms are developed and managed in-house by a dedicated team of data science specialists. We have come a long way from using a pocket calculator to analyse figures gathered from company reports to using machines which decide which stocks to be picked for investing. PrathitBhobe, MD & CEO, Tata Asset Management said, "Machines have massive computational power needed to process very large data sets, spot patterns and correlations, make decisions faster, objectively and without human biases. In the current world, computers are powerful enough to solve problems, a lot of data is available and we strive to use this data in combination with algorithms to its best". "Tata Mutual Fund has developed intelligent machine-driven strategies keeping in mind the appetite of long-term equity investors. This framework crunches massive amounts of data, recognises patterns and leverages the power of technology. The future of investing is in the use of quants and with us entering a new decade, we believe that the Indian market is now ready for tech-based investing", says Sailesh Jain, Fund Manager, Tata Asset Management According to UtpalSarma, Head – Business Analytics, Tata Asset Management, "Actively managed funds benefit from human intelligence that learn, comprehend, and respond to different market challenges in complex manners. Passively managed funds, on the other hand, are rule based and they avoid pitfalls of biases that accompany human judgement. Their strength lies in increased objectivity and elimination of human errors. These traditional styles have contrasting pros and cons. AI and ML adds a third dimension to fund management. They enable machines to mimic human judgement to certain extent while retaining the benefits of disciplined rule-based investing. Investment strategies employing such constructs tend to leverage market opportunities better while avoiding bias errors. Technologies supporting artificial intelligence today is quite evolved and robust. Their wide usage across businesses is testimony of their potential and capability. While quant strategies for wealth management features prominently in advanced markets, its only a matter of time that they gain popularity in India as well" The minimum application amount for this fund is Rs. 5,000/- and in multiples of Re.1/- thereafter and additional investment of Rs 1,000/- and in multiples of Re 1/- thereafter. The fund will be managed by Mr. Sailesh Jain. Tata Quant Fund is available with our digital channel partners Paytm Money &Groww App.

Title: Transformation of financial business processes & future opportunities in the Fintech space
Content:
Hemant Chafale,
CEO- Trust Systems & Software Pvt. Ltd.

1. How the breakthrough technologies like AI, Blockchain, intelligent automation and IoT are reshaping the financial services space in India?
In terms of customer behaviour management, in terms of offering various financial services, IoT, although it's not that predominant right now, but in coming days, most other things will be machine driven rather than the human intervention and AI is going to play very, very crucial role in giving feedback mechanism to the entire applications so that the services will be improved, customer will have multiple choice and thereby the cost, end of the day is going to come down. Today it's typically 2 percent, which is substantially high.
With automation and all these AI and IoT, the operational cost should come down to 0.5 percent, which will be benefit to customer as well as to the bank.

<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/zRk7pZwI4fQ" width="560" height="315" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen"></iframe>

• Please talk about few use-cases where these technologies have transformed the financial business processes and overall customer experience?
Some of the finance companies, they are using this AI for offering multiple products to the customers and they're able to acquire those customers online. Like if you see you'll find a lot of messages coming to you, pre- sanction loans coming to you. These are all basically inputs from various credit agencies, your behavioural pattern, surfing pattern. All these data captured and based on the intelligence, the offers are made to the customer.

2. Please talk about the operational and financial benefits Fintech solutions offer to SMB and enterprise customers?
Both SMB and Enterprise behave differently.
For the enterprise or the industry expects that there has to be end to end solution for its employees, for its own organization and for its customer. What SMB typically, it is a cost and the service which matters. So, when we talk of fintech and latest platform and the technology, the service turn- around time has drastically reduced.
Most of the things are automated just like KYC. Earlier, it used to happen that the account opening itself used to take two to three days. Now it's a matter of few minutes, your account gets open. NEFT has started 24/7, very shortly RTGS will also start 24/7.
So, basically banking will be 365 days 24 by 7.
Branch operations, probably may get reduced to five days working, which will also increase the service to the entire community as well as to the banking industry.

3. Payments have been at the forefront of India’s Fintech revolution with UPI, mobile wallets, mobile banking growing aggressively. What are the emerging trends in the digital payments segment in India?
Although, you find a lot of ATMs, cards. But going forward, cards may not be required. Your mobile becomes your digital payment system. Your QR code will suffice the needs of payment and authentication. Slowly, we are moving to card less economy and maybe very shortly a cashless economy.

4. InsuranceTech and WealthTech are also finding great acceptance with the growing Fintech space. What are the emerging trends in these segments?
Once the customer is acquired because of the technology and because of the various options available, every fintech company or a bank wants to provide a maximum solution through the same customer and thereby increasing their bottom line. That's why fintech are now moving on to insurance segment where the risk is low and turn- around time is also low.

5. With the boom in digital transactions, the security of customers’ payment data has become extremely crucial. How are we securing the digital transactions and customers’ data?
New trend is coming. RBI has mandated some of the masking of master data.
The encryption, earlier used to be 64bit data encryption. Now it is mandatory that you have 256 kb of data encryption and VAPT: Vulnerable Assessment Penetration Testing. Every instance, every installation is mandated by RBI.
It has to be VAPT compliant, so a lot of security. PCIDSS compliance has also come up.
Now at every point, the secrecy, security and the penetration is very important. RBI is controlling all these and ensuring that their data is safe and secure.

6. What are the challenges that exist in the Fintech space in India?
The biggest challenge is that people still feel that bigger infrastructure, bigger banks are required.
In the Western world, the banks are changing. Entire banking is now moving on mobile.
In next 10 years, we will find there'll be a banking, but there will not be big infrastructure for the bank. There'll be a digital infrastructure.

7. What are the opportunities IT channel partners have in the Fintech space? How can they address their customers’ financial requirements with the partnership with Fintech players?
It's always good to have partnership with fintech players and in I.T. space, it's always the authenticity, secrecy, commitment of the partner. Is service commitment to the customer because of which he gives business.
So, if he has a relationship, then the partner relationship with customer works with fintech will definitely give better results.

8. What are the future opportunities you see in the Fintech space in India?
In terms of digitization, there's going to be a paperless banking, all documentation. Government is planning to have digilocker, so you will find that it is completely, 100% paper less. Right now we have a location for the branch, for the customer. Once it becomes digital, all their documents will be authenticated using the document I.D. at the digilocker. A lot of paperwork will move out. It'll be anywhere bank, serviced by person, sitting anywhere and service given at any location.
It'll be independent of geography, product and it will definitely reduce substantial cost, end of the day of the service.

Title: Cybercrime takes another hit as Jamtara fraudsters dupe a wallet user posing a Paytm Executive
Content:
A Mumbai-based Paytm Customer has been duped of INR 1.7 Lakh by a gang whose kingpin is from Jamtara District in Jharkand. The gang managed to get hold of the customer’s account on the pretext of updating his know your customer (KYC) details.

As per a report, a message was sent by the gang from an unknown number to the Paytm user, asking him to provide his KYC details or else his Paytm account will be blocked. The message also contained a contact number.

As soon as the victim dialled the number, he was asked to download Team Viewer (a screen sharing tool) and send Re.1 to any Paytm user. The screensharing tool could easily help them get hold on his login details. Even before the Paytm Customer could hang up the phone, INR 1.72 Lakh got withdrawn from his bank account.

As per the revelations of the Police investigation, one of the accused Big Bazaar cash vouchers worth INR 50K and forwarded it to other 3 gang members who further bought 70 mobile phones and later sold them in Lower Parel and Grand Road in Mumbai.

Three of the accused have been arrested by the Police on January 14 and the search for other gang members including the kingpin is still going on.

Vijay Shekhar, Founder at Paytm had also tweeted about such frauds in November 2019. His tweet highlighted one such SMSes. The decision turned out post Paytm’s cyber cell and the RBI ombudsman came in terms with a few fraud related complaints from its users.

Recently the records suggest that six Paytm users were deceived of INR 5.04 Lakh by Fraudsters pretending to be Paytm employees. One of the users also mentioned that he got a call from the scamster asking him to update his KYC and execute a payment of Rs. 10 in the ‘Quick Support’ app for the same purpose.

Notably they also asked the user to share his Pan and Aadhaar card number post which the user lost more than INR 1.2 Lakh. Similar instances have been noticed by 5 Paytm users in Mohali who received calls and December 2019 and January 2020.

According to a cyber officer from Mumbai Police, this kind of cybercrime is trending since a year. 40 such numbers have been noted by them. The calls are reportedly from Jamtara in Jharkand which is known as the hub of cyber crimes and frauds. Apart from Jamtara two three more places in North Indian states have been traced from where these calls are being made.

Title: RBI rolls out new rules for Credit and Debit Cards
Content:
New rules have been introduced by the Reserve Bank of India to enhance the security features of credit and debit cards. Banks are responsible for ensuring that before the cards are issued or reissued, they are enabled only for domestic transactions at PoS terminals as well as ATMs.

As per the announcement by the RBI, the cards (physical or virtual) at the time of its issue should be enabled for use just at the contact-based points of usage within the country.

If customers are willing to use their cards for contactless transactions, online transactions and international transactions, they need to separately apply for such services.

The regulator stated that in case a customer has not previously availed his or her cards for contactless, online or international transactions then their card will be disabled for these services. In order to avail these facilities, the customer will have to apply to the respective banks. As far as the existing card users are concerned banks can take the necessary action weather to disable the card for domestic as well as international transactions, contactless and online transaction rights on the basis of their risk perception.

The Central Bank reportedly stated that cards which have never been in use for online, contactless or international transactions shall be compulsorily disabled for this purpose.

Banks will have to ensure that the cardholders get to ‘switch off’ or ‘switch on the online, international as well as contactless transaction at the ATMs and PoS terminals. One will also be enabled to set their own limit for every kind of transaction at the ATMs. An option should also be available for the customers for opting any of these services via 24*7 net banking or mobile applications. Any change in status of the card must be informed to the customers by the Bank through email or SMS alerts.

The Central bank further added that rules of this sort will not be applicable on prepaid gift cards as well as those cards which are used at mass transit system. It will be from March 16 that these new rules for debit and credit cards will come into effect.

Title: Re-inventing Finance - Jeetender Singh, CFO- Napino Auto & Electronics Ltd
Content:
“Consumer focus, digital transformation and M&As are three areas where finance has reinvented itself” - Jeetender Singh, CFO- Napino Auto & Electronics Ltd How is the finance function reinventing itself in most enterprises? Reinventing finance, has happened in most organizations in three buckets. The first is how the finance function is transforming itself from being shareholder value focused to becoming consumer centric. Increasingly, more and more organizations are becoming aware of the fact that long term value is created for an organization if you are consumer centric.  Subsequently shareholder value gets automatically delivered. Second is digital transformation. How AI, ML robotics automation are impacting the finance function? This does require a lot of retooling, re-skilling the orientation of the core finance and accounting folks. Thirdly, mergers and acquisitions and how finance function works around that area. Finance function has actually transformed itself from being a score keeper, ready to be very proactive in almost setting up the rules of the game within organizations. Traditionally finance function was kind of walking in the background. Now, finance team is part of the core strategy of the company. They focus on how/ what the company should be doing, what should be the resource allocation and how the future strategy of the company should be derived given the markets have become more and more dynamic?
  • 2. What are the operational benefits you have observed with the fintech solutions in your organization?
We are more of a traditional company, but we did work with at least one fintech startup. They basically work with providing a solution for the smaller vendors. The large vendors we have may have issues in an immediate financing. We have certain payment terms. So this is where these guys come in and they are able to offer immediate credit, immediate payment to the suppliers. They come in where there is a credit crunch for the SMBs or MSMEs.  They provide immediate credit to them and based on the invoice they do invoice discounting. Banks at times are not willing to work that way, and take that risk on their books. So, they come in and they play that role. It is quite an innovative solution. Let us see how that works.

Title: RBI releases minutes of its board meeting held in October
Multiple losses lead to Vodafone m-pesa shutting down
Content:
Whereas India’s digital payments sector seems to be booming like never before, the circumstances of certain banks tells the other side of the fintech story. This has come into light more by Vodafone m-pesa shutting down. An announcement made by the RBI on Tuesday suggests that there has been a cancellation of the certificate of authorization (CoA) of Vodafone, m-pesa on account of the company’s voluntary surrender.

RBI post this cancellation stated that the company will not be allowed to carry out operation and issuance of prepaid payment instruments (PPIs).

As the company shuts down its operation post the official closure, RBI has informed its customer or merchants who are somehow associated with Vodafone m-pesa can approach the company for the settlement of their claims up to three years from now i.e January 21, 2020.

In a recent report by RBI- “Trend and Progress of Banking in India”, it has been stated that the Indian payments banks (PBs) have notably registered a 21% hike in their losses from Rs. 512 Cr in FY2019 to Rs. 626.8 in FY19, ending March 2019.

The RBI notes the fact as well that payments banks hold a very limited operational space and the expense of setting up the infrastructure seems quite high. Hence, it is tough for payments bank to break even, despite gaining new customers, which is now gradually leading many of these banks to shut down its operations.

Hardly a year after the launch of Aditya Idea Payments Bank, it had to decide to shut down the company and currently the organization is proceeding towards its liquidation in July 2019.

Vodafone m-pesa and Aditya Birla Idea Payments Banks we among the 11 payments bank who had received the licence from the Reserve Bank of India under Section 22 (1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 for carrying out the business of payments bank in India.

Apart from these two companies, four more operators in the payments bank sector are having to shut down their operation in India. The list includes Cholamandalam Investment and Finance Company, Tech Mahindra, a Consortium Backed by Sun Pharma founder Dilip Shanghvi, IDFC Bank and Telenor Financial Services.

Title: The FinTech Transformation
Content: The post demonetization era saw the rise of Indian financial services industry, with an amalgamation of various sectors into one — the FinTech. Explore with us the whole ecosystem, emerging models and upcoming opportunities for IT channel Kalpana Singhal The demonetization drive in 2016 in India can safely be called the landmark moment which redefined the FinTech ecosystem as it was understood until then and put many FinTech startups in India on the map. The ban on Rs 500 and Rs 1,000 currency notes, which wiped out 86.4 percent of cash from the economy overnight, forced the public to switch to digital payments and online transactions en-masse. It was this impetus to the wave of digitization that led to the boom of the existing digital payments platforms and the founding of new ones. While the existing players went on to achieve soaring valuations, new FinTech startups quickly scrambled to fill in the existing opportunity, and bring technology to the many sub-sectors of FinTech. Today, FinTech has expanded to include any technological innovation in — and automation of — the financial sector. This includes advances in financial literacy, advice and education, as well as streamlining of wealth management, lending and borrowing, retail banking, fundraising, money transfers/payments, investment management and more. “The FinTech industry in India is rapidly expanding, and the adoption rate is growing faster than anticipated. One of the reasons for strong growth is that traditional financial services companies have entered the fray in a big way,” says Mahesh Makhija, Partner and Leader, Digital and Emerging Tech, EY, in a press statement. The ecosystem India’s evolution as a progressive FinTech nation is not a miracle. It happened at the back of executing a four-point approach. Firstly, solving for identity in the form of Aadhaar for formalization. Secondly, getting everyone a bank account to store money. Thirdly, building scalable platform(s) to move money (IMPS, UPI, etc.). And finally, allowing banks and FinTech organizations and wealth/insurance/lending players also to access platform like UPI to innovate. This framework has led India to a FinTech revolution. As per a NASSCOM report, in 2018 there were around 400 FinTech companies operating in India; this number is constantly growing. NASSCOM predicts that the revenue generated in India from FinTech companies will touch $2.4 billion by 2020. The Indian FinTech market has seen the emergence of a few dominant segments that are disrupting the financial services value chain by offering technology-led innovations to improve customer experience and engagement, and to drive operational efficiency. Within this space, digital payments and alternative lending have emerged as the most mature segments, driven by sustained funding, Government support and huge untapped market opportunities. Almost 75 percent of Indian FinTechs are either in lending or payments. In 2018, lending continued to be the hottest sub-sector, mopping up half the equity funding invested in Indian FinTech ecosystem. As per the recent analysis, digital payments are just about 13 percent of the total volume and currently, 87 percent of the transactions happen through cash. Thus, FinTech is a lucrative sector to invest in and is set to grow exponentially in the India growth market. Payments Payments have been at the forefront of India’s digital revolution, with digital payment transaction volumes (worth $3.5 trillion) touching approximately 24.13 billion in 2018. The demonetization drive launched in November 2016 and lucrative returns on mobile wallets and UPI transactions (which led to their widespread adoption) have been key to driving exponential growth in digital transactions. In addition, the rise of digital commerce, innovation in payments technology using AI, blockchain, the Internet of Things (IoT) and real-time payments; and the introduction of mobile point of sale (POS) devices have led to a reduction in the cost of acceptance infrastructure and also contributed to growth. “Digital payments have been in the foray of bringing the unbanked population into the mainstream. Linking wallets such as Paytm to UPI has made transactions much simpler and apt. Going forward, these would start working as a full-fledged marketplace and also emerge as change agents for digital economy,” highlights Ritesh Varma, Global Head, Business Solutions, Newgen Software. The emerging trend in digital payment is interoperability. “You can make payment in a secure manner directly from your mobile phone through various applications. Most companies are now trying to understand how they can use your payment data as well as app usage frequency to enable various utility apps to go beyond just making bill payment or recharges,” adds Dev Ramnane, VP & Business Head, B2B Business, ClearTax India. Alternative lending Technology-driven alternative lenders are upending the traditional lending value chain by engaging in both product and process innovation to improve customer experience and drive operational efficiency. These new-age lenders employ advanced technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) to optimize their customer acquisition process for reducing costs, incorporate alternative data for credit underwriting and adopt sophisticated risk management solutions for vastly improving downstream lending activities, including collections management and loan resolution. The number of business models that surround the alternative lending space is on the rise every day, both locally and globally. Broadly it can fall in to two categories, consumer lending and SME lending. For consumer lending, the emerging business models include peer to peer marketplace, all types of term-loans, payday loans and line of credit. “Some startups in this space also provide easy check out options for the customers during an online/offline purchase. In addition, the entire customer on-boarding and loan disbursement processes including application submission, eKYC, credit scoring, underwriting and disbursement are done online. There are many startups which specialize in providing one or more of these processes as a standalone service to BFSI organizations and thus have built their business models around the same. In the B2B segment, the emerging models include supply chain finance, invoice discounting, working capital loans and crowd-funding to name a few,” details Suresh Narayanan, Product Strategist and Fintech Consultant & Former Head of Product, AssetVault.   In the B2B lending space, supply chain finance is an emerging area. “If a company requires working capital loans, in the supply chain finance there is a concept called invoice discounting. This is where you already have an invoice that you have sent to the client, they will give you early payment and the customer will get discount and the vendor instead of waiting for 60-90 days for payment will get immediate payment,” shares Ramnane. He further highlights that few models will emerge around GST. “As GST has access to all of the data, we will see models to analyze the flow of invoices and cash. That can enable us to underwrite the customer in a better way and reduce the cost of underwriting, making it more accurate and reduce the NPAs by using GST data.” InsurTech  With the emerging InsurTech landscape, global insurance firms are offering customized solutions by leveraging data like tailor-made health policies based on customer’s orientation towards remaining fit. Few startups are also exploring the integration of AR to smoothen the consumer experience towards automobiles claims. Few firms also operate on differentiated business models where the total policy amount is pooled centrally and used to pay off claims and the remaining balance determines the next premium amount for all policyholders. InsurTech landscape is quite nascent in India at this stage. The current insurance penetration is quite low at 3.69 percent, compared to the global average of 6.5 percent. Some of the key areas that need to be developed for better adoption of digital insurance in India are AI/ML-based underwriting assessment that can better assess the risk and improve the loss ratio. In addition, IoT-based preventive insurance solutions can result in proactive customer engagement and premium, and claims reductions for both insurers and insured. Armed with the capabilities of AI/ML, predictive analytics, and data captured by IoT-driven connected devices, InsurTech players are exploring ways to make the most out of deep data insights and drive the transition from a reactive approach to proactive prevention. Preventive insurance providers are gaining significant traction, across the entire insurance value chain from health insurance to home/equipment/ transit/automotive insurance. The newer business models, such as micro-insurance on-demand, are changing the nature of the insurance industry by moving from complex long-term insurance products to short-term insurance products based on time, usage, and activity. The focus on the niche segments is driving this trend and enabling the rise of innovative, tech-driven InsurTech players in these areas. Collaboration is the Key In the context of the compete-vs-collaborate debate, the increasing trust in the financial services ecosystem has brought traditional financial service providers, IT channel partners and FinTech players together to explore more opportunities for collaboration. These partnerships have led to innovative customer propositions and new revenue streams – traditional partners adopt technology and innovation in a more seamless and rapid cycle, while FinTech players symbiotically increase their presence through the distribution infrastructure of IT channel partners. “The whole space is going to work on a partnership approach. Gone are the days when anybody can say that they will do it all by themselves. Not from just the investment and cost perspective, but even from the changing technology perspective, you need a technology partner who has the ability to bring in emerging and upcoming technologies,” shares Ramesh Iyer, Vice Chairman and MD, Mahindra Finance.   IT channel partners can serve as aggregators for FinTech players and provide access to the end customers. “They can leverage the FinTech partnerships to address the financial requirements of end customers by giving them access to various FinTech solutions like peer-to-peer lending and so on,” adds Varma. Girish Kannalli, Vice President and General Manager, Insurance and Healthcare BU, InfoGain, highlights that leveraging API (Application Programing Interfaces) will enable greater collaboration between traditional financial companies and the non-financial companies to provide greater services to the customers. “FinTech is creating huge opportunities for companies with capital to collaborate with companies who have customers to offer broad range of services.” The parting thought During a recent address, Amitabh Kant, CEO, Niti Aayog, highlighted that FinTech market in India is likely to expand to $31 billion in 2020. He further said that India is one of the fastest growing FinTech markets globally. India is the only country in the world with over a billion mobile connections and biometrics, providing enough scope for penetration of FinTech technology, Kant highlights. "The Indian FinTech ecosystem is the third largest globally. Over $6 billion investments have already happened in FinTech market in the country in the last 3-4 years," he adds. Bringing it all together, the FinTech revolution is slowly collaborating all the existing technologies in one complex environment. While digitization is the beginning of the revolution, it is further leading the millennials to the future comprising smart homes, smart cities, smart contracts, open banking and much more. The adoption of blockchain and cryptocurrency will just add a finishing touch thereby bridging the FinTech startups, banks, finance institutions and consumers in one loop. Definitely, the future with FinTech is worth looking forward to!

Title: FinTech Liberation for MSMEs
Content: Despite of exclusive legislations and policies, MSMEs have failed to reach their full potential owing to lack of access to formal credit. For lenders, the fragmented and opaque nature of available MSME information poses a serious challenge for underwriting. Other factors, including a lack of collateral and formal credit ratings, coupled with high transaction costs, act as a further disincentive to lend to MSMEs. However, this situation is set to change with huge improvements in digital infrastructure and the roll-out of structural reforms such as the GST rollout. As a result, MSME businesses will be formalized through the increased availability of digital MSME information that can be utilized for credit assessment. In fact, the operational benefits that FinTech solutions offer to MSME and SMB customers are numerous. The entire application and disbursement processes are completely online reducing the hassle of taking multiple trips to the Bank/NBFC branches, thereby reducing the TAT for any loan application process. The presence of multiple FinTech players and online marketplace are enabling competitive rates and transparent pricing. “In terms of the financial benefits, the operational costs saved due to automation of manual processes in the longer run will be passed on to the customer as lesser processing fees. The most important benefit that FinTech solutions offer is the easy availability of credit,” adds Suresh Narayanan, Product Strategist and Fintech Consultant & Former Head of Product, AssetVault. Ritesh Varma, Global Head, Business Solutions, Newgen Software, further adds that with the advent of automation and technologies such as AI and analytics, MSMEs can be better underwritten for prospective frauds and early warning systems can be in place for quick and timely addressal.

Title: New-Age Tech Push for FinTech
Content: As organizations are reshaping their business models to take advantage of emerging technologies, the risk-management function is also undergoing a paradigm shift to keep pace with these developments. Advanced technologies like ML and cloud computing have made it possible for organizations to analyze vast amounts of data, both structured and unstructured, to accurately uncover and assess emerging risks and drive optimum pricing strategies. Further, heightened regulatory scrutiny in the financial services space and increased costs for compliance breaches are also driving organizations to build sophisticated risk management capabilities to effectively navigate in an increasingly open and connected world. AI, ML, blockchain, AR and IoT have served significant use cases for FinTech growth globally. Blockchain driven banking solutions are successful in the US, UK, Singapore and can see penetration in India. AI- and ML-driven data points to generate credit and risk profile of customers also have tremendous potential to boom. Some of the common use cases of AI across FinTech are credit analysis, risk management, fraud prevention, and enabling personal services. These are effectively helping the enterprises reduce the overall time to make decisions with minimal risks and effectively prevent fraud. In addition, intelligent automation has been leveraged significantly to cut operational costs and boost productivity. Robotic process automation is taking over the repetitive and mundane tasks; meaning that bots are faster, cutting down the time required to close such a job. AI enables companies to re-route their workforce to more meaningful activities, highlights Girish Kannalli, Vice President and General Manager, Insurance and Healthcare BU, InfoGain.   Businesses are using AI and Bot technology to automate a lot of the repetitive task including form-15, tax returns as well as in GST filling. “GST has mandated for invoice-level matching, in the absence of which the input tax credit is not provided. Here we are employing an AI-based technology to improve the level of matching and avoid any typo error,” shares Dev Ramnane, VP & Business Head, B2B Business, ClearTax India.   Further, banks are using blockchain to improve their 'Know Your Customer’ (KYC) and implement 'anti-money laundering (AML) regulations. “Increased adoption of blockchain helps address the security concerns as well as reduce the overall transactional cost and speed of transactions by eliminating intermediaries. Clearing and settlement, cross border payments are good examples of other use cases where the finance industry can leverage this technology,” suggests Kannalli.

Title: Tech in financial services is opening channel partner prospects.
Content:
India’s financial technology sector may be younger, but is developing hastily, serviced by a big marketplace base, an innovation oriented startup landscape, and friendly government guidelines and ordinances. Fintech market in India is likely to expand to $31 billion in 2020, Niti Aayog CEO Amitabh Kant said at an event organised by industry body Assocham, recently. He further said India is one of the fastest growing fintech markets globally and that the Indian fintech ecosystem is the third largest in the globe. $6 billion investments have already happened in fintech market in the country in the last 3-4 years. India is the only country in the world with over a billion mobile connections and biometrics, providing enough scope for penetration of fintech technology.

Also, the National Association of Software and Services Companies (NASSCOM) pronounced in 2019 that round 400 fintech companies operated in India, boosted in large part by means of overseas investments in fintech-focused startup accelerators and incubators.

With smartphone penetration anticipated to growth to 85 -90 percent in 2020 from 65- 75 percentage currently, and net penetration steadily rising, the boom potential for fintech in India cannot be overstated.

Fintech startups want to instill more self-assurance among Indian customers, already known for being conservative in their economic possibilities.

Technologies like AI in financial services is opening channel partner prospects, from building customer service chatbots to creating a better customer on boarding process.

Financial enterprises now work with more information than ever before. However, they often have trouble using that data for a competitive advantage. Enter AI and machine learning tools that automate data analysis. Here's an overview of some currently prominent applications for AI in financial services.

Financial services companies need to protect valuable assets, so fraud detection is one area where AI use is common. In the customer service field, much of the early AI work focused on back-office procedures to provide clients easier access to their account information. But there's a shift underway.

AI has begun having an impact on the front office. AI can help financial services firms get new customers in the system, as well as fill the sales funnel. Many financial services organizations are deploying chatbots, which have varying levels of sophistication. Automation through RPA can help Financial services firms save a lot of time of collecting information for auditing and compliance reports. Financial services employees continuously use information to make financial decisions wherein, AI and machine learning algorithms analyze data and make recommendations and increasingly decisions about such transactions.

But deploying AI in financial services is not easy. Building a data model entails the right mix of art and science.  Therefore, an organization first needs to understand its own data integrity issues. Then with the help of AI or machine learning applications can do garbage in, garbage out.

Title: Quicko, an online tax filing platform raises funds from Zerodha's Rainmatte seed funding
Content:
INR 2 Crores have been raised by Quicko, Ahmedabad based online income tax filing platform. These funds have been reportedly gained from Rainmatter Capital in Seed funding.

The funds which have been arranged will be further utilized by the start-ups to establish  its own tax filing service for the online trading community which is to be integrated with Zerodha for enabling its customers to upload and file their income tax returns.

Rainmatter has been rolled out by Zerodha, an online stock trading start-up which focused on funding as well as incubating innovative fintech startups in India.

The last investment by Rainmatter is reportedly their fifteenth such investment. Rainmatter so far has invested in startups like option trading platform Sensibull, micro savings platform Balance, credit card bill payment app CRED, thematic investment platform Small case and online marketplace for fixed income instruments GoldenPi.

Quicko was founded in 2015 by Vishvajit Sonagara. The company focuses on simplifying taxes for both businesses and individuals through its tax preparation, planning and filing platform. Since the Start-up has a freemium model, it manages to enable its users to file their own income tax returns free of cost with just one fee which is required to import their financial and investment data.

Quicko claims to have helped more than 11,000 traders in filing their income tax returns in the last one head. The startup in the coming year aspires to help 100,000 traders and hold the position of a leading platform for online tax filing in the country.

While discussing about the benefits of the platform, Founder of Quick, Vishwajit Sonagara reportedly stated that their platform immensely reduces the cost so much that they are being able to offer it to the traders at merely Rs. 2,500 in comparison to Rs. 15,000-20,000 that a CA would charge them in any traditional market. This platform serves as a solution for many first time traders.

Notably there are certain competitors of Quicko which exist in the Indian market and there names are myITreturn, H&R Block India and ClearTax.

Title: How do cost cutting strategies map out future planning? | Akhil Handa, Bank of Baroda
Content: “VR and AR are augmenting the financial industry by the way of customer service delivery” –How critical is fraud detection in the finance vertical? This is a big pain area now. In the Reserve Bank report there is mention about Rs 70,000 crore of fraud that has been detected over the last few years. And typically, detection of fraud happens with a time lag of about 5-6 years. You will need to be more proactive about it. The Reserve Bank has directed the banks to institute a range of cheques. All banks are directed to do it; we are also doing it. With the help of those, frauds will get detected and identified a lot earlier than we are now doing it actually. Akhil Handa, Head (Fintech, Partnerships & Mobile Banking), Bank of Baroda   How is the VR and AR disrupting the Finance Industry? VR and AR are augmenting what we have in financial industry by the way of customer service delivery. I think, these technologies go on to further augment the experience customers have and make it more delightful for them to engage with us. How do cost cutting strategies map out for future planning? We are under a three way merger process right now where Bank of Baroda, Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank are getting amalgamated. One of the core pillars of this amalgamation is deriving cost energies. And there is a replication and triplication in this case of administrative units, offices, administrative staff, IT, license, data centers. These are replicated over and over again. Time has come to rationalize some of these cost and overheads. The Government strategy of merging some of the banks to make banks to a much larger scale is a step in the right direction.

Title: Consumer lending start-up MoneyTap raises 500 crore in a Series B funding round
Content:
A statement by the consumer lending start-up MoneyTap, it has raised 500 crore in a Series B funding round which was led by Aquiline Technology Growth, RTP Global and Sequoia India.

Other participators were existing investors MegaDelta and Prime Venture Partners. So far, the start-up has reportedly raised $12.3 million, keeping the current round aside.

The funds will be utilised by the company in growing its loan book to ₹5,000 crore in the upcoming 12-18 months, invest in data science, technology and roll out its own non-banking financial company (NBFC). Further the start-up has other plans too of expanding its footprint from 60 to 200 Indian cities.

The lending start-up is known for offering easy access to credit through a mobile app and is majorly aimed at working professionals. The app proposes instant loans beginning from 3,000 to 5 lakh, charging interest of 15-19% per Anum.

What else MoneyTap offers in credit in the form of a ‘credit-line’ with a choice to secure an instant predetermined uncollateralized loan. The start-up is one of the growing numbers of tech-start-ups which are into the use of alternative credit score to underwrite borrowers. Banks generally depend on credit scores which are supplied by credit bureaus to underwrite loan applications, but at times the scores may portray an inaccurate indicator of a borrower’s creditworthiness.

MoneyTap and other new-age lenders collect customer data such as salary slips, bank statements, information such as contacts and text messages stored in a person’s phone and location data to further underwrite

Potential borrowers.

The start-up was founded in 2015 and it claims to have made a loan books of 1,000 crore and attain an annual disbursal run rate 2,500 crore in the past three years. The NBFC licence also got secured by MoneyTap in September 2019.

Title: Syncordisis Grantedthe ‘Support Professionals of the Financial Sector’Status by Luxembourg Ministry of Finance
Content: ‘Support PSF’ status enables Syncordis to provide locally hosted SaaS services, and strengthens its position as a Temenos Global Services Partner Syncordis PSF S.A.,a leading Temenos banking software specialist and a subsidiary of Larsen & Toubro Infotech Ltd. (LTI) has been granted‘Support Professional of the Financial Sector’ (Support PSF, Art 29-3 - OSIP) licensebyLuxembourg Ministry of Finance. A Professional of the Financial Sector ("PSF") is an entity that is authorized to perform financial sector activities as a regular occupation, in accordance with article 13 of the law.The licensestrengthens Syncordis’ position as a Temenos Global Services Partner and is valid for an unlimited duration. The PSF status serves as a guarantee for clients as every PSF Support company must comply with regulatory requirements, be financially stable, and implement a highest level of quality in terms of organization, infrastructure, security and internal controls. Stéphane Fisch,Managing Directorand Head of Managed Services,SyncordisPSF S.A. said, “We have provided onsite production services since 2008, but the growing demand for outsourced production support services and SaaS solutions for Temenos clients called for this strategic move. Syncordis PSF will provide end-to-end managed services to its clients with the highest standards of security, governance, processes and tools. Obtaining the “Support PSF” license marks a major milestone forSyncordisand will give us a competitive edge to add unprecedented value todigital transformation journeys of our clients.” Sudhir Chaturvedi, President & Executive Board Member, LTI said, “I congratulate Syncordis on this remarkable accomplishment. Syncordis PSF now has full rights to operate primary information systems in the banking sector and can take full responsibility to operate financial institutions’ production environment. This setup enables Syncordis’ clients to fully focus on their core business without worrying about technology and enjoy multiple additional benefits such as locally hosted SaaS solutions, increased transparency and security as well as appropriate management of direct and indirect risks.” Luxembourgian companies that apply for a PSF license must undergo a lengthy application process with the CSSF. Syncordis started the process in 2018 and submitted 1.500 pagesworth of documents over the course of the past two years to comply with and meet all CSSF requirements. Licensed companies are audited yearly and must report to the CSSF on a monthly basis

Title: Blockchain 2.0 in banking and fintech | Devendra Sharma | Bank Of India
Content:
• How block chain technology is working in the banking and fintech sector? What is its potential and challenge?
What has happened so far in blockchain technology as far as banking is concerned  is a perceptible shift in a way, the bankers or the fintech industry is now looking at blockchain technology. Initially when it came, there was a huge amount of excitement related to blockchain technology as such. Devendra Sharma, Chief Vigilance Officer, Bank of India.   The things have changed over a period of time. Initially, everybody used to ask a question as to why this blockchain technology should be adopted in our particular industry. Now the questioning has changed. Now people over a period of time have started asking how this blockchain technology can be utilized in our sector. That's a huge shift. And initially when the why question was that there was a lot of cynicism. There was a lot of excitement. And everybody thought about  going on board and adopting this technology. Then people understood that this technology is not the Bitcoin that we are talking of or it is not only the crypto cryptocurrency related technology. But this technology can be utilized even by the service providers who were the present intermediaries and who are providing services to the commercial organizations. So if a banker is engaged in a trade finance model, if he is providing a trade finance module or a solution to their clients, where one is an importer and another is an exporter and they reside in two different countries, there are a lot of compliance issues which include the compliance of the regulators of both the countries and also certain trust related issues about the movement of goods, about the quality of the goods and the certification agencies of these two parts. The idea of blockchain was to have a system in place where all the parties subscribe to this particular transaction. And with the distributed ledger at all ledges of the transaction, they are in a position to have a complete view, independent view on whatever is going on in that particular transaction. So once that realization has come, now the solutions for other similar type of activities like remittances, which can be done so with least of inter mediation, excess of the trust amongst the parties and shortening of the time and the labor in a transaction is mainly which is looked at. So there's a huge possibility in the sector. The banking sector is very, very enthusiastic about it. A few of the banks, a few of the Indian private banks as well as the public sector banks have come together and they are looking into some solutions.  
  • Do you think these technologies will obliterate the fraudulent transactions?
When all the parties are in place for a particular transaction with goes through on a blockchain technology, the chances of a cheating happening by any of the players turning bad actor is more or less obliterated. When I say more or less, the more is the higher percentage. But as you say, that nothing is perfect in this world. So I would say that okay, a very, very less percentage of chances are there that any cheating or any misdeed can happen.

Title: YAP secures INR 10 Cr from Kunal Shah, Citrus Founders and others
Content:
YAP-a Chennai based platform has reportedly secured INR 10 Cr. In an angel funding round. YAP’s parent company, M2P Solutions has reportedly raised the amount from Amrish Rau, former PayU India CEO, Founder of Cred Kunal Shah, Founder of Jupiter Jitendra Gupta FinTech MeetUp’s Abhishant Pant, Venture Capitalist of 8i Ventures and Karbon’s Peifu Hsieh.

According to YAP cofounder Madhusudanan R, the recent funds will be utilised in the company’s expansion. The tram will be expanded as well as new banking products for fintech start-ups will be developed. Rau will also be joining the board of M2P solutions as part of this deal.

YAP was founded in 2014 and it helps fintech start-ups in rapidly developing and launching their own payment solutions. It offers financial solutions like issuing physical or virtual prepaid card, git cards that its clients can give to their users. QR code solutions are also offered to its clients.

YAP has got associated with banks like DCB Bank, Yes Bank, Equitas SFB and SBM Bank for the SPI platform which they offer to their clients. Certain clients who use YAP’s platforms include Bank Open, Ola, Cred, Slice, Redcarpet and Niyo among others.

As per claims made by the company it has processed payments of more than $2 Bn last year. It even claims to have processed more than 50 Mn transactions which is a remarkable growth of 300% in comparison to the previous year. In fact, the company says that it will use the funds in adding more fintech clients.

A NITI Aayog report called Digital Payments (2018 edition) suggests that India’s digital payments industry is predicted to touch $1 Tn by 2023. As per the report’s highlights the value of digital payments is expected to jump from the present 10% to over 25 % by 2023.

Nevertheless, with UPI’s introduction in the digital payment space has brought a huge transformation in the Indian fintech sector along with the increasing internet penetration.

Investors with this burgeoning growth have started to remain bullish on start-ups working in this segment. SuperMoney, fintech start-up earlier this month raised $1 Mn in Pre-Series A funding from Unitus Ventures, an early-stage investor.

Before this, serial entrepreneurs, Shailaz Nag’s new start-up Dot had secured $8 Mn in seed funding. Dot is notably a technology start-up known for providing novel digital transformation along with commerce solutions to brick and mortar outlets.

Title: Fintech in India: Rapid Progress, But Miles to go
Content:
Aditya Agarwal, Co-Founder, Wealthy elaborates how digitization has changed the paradigm of the financial services industry in India, but cautions that fintech has till now only touched a minority of the Indian population.  
  1. How the breakthrough technologies like AI, Blockchain, intelligent automation and IoT are reshaping the financial services space in India? Please talk about few use-cases where these technologies have transformed the financial business processes and overall customer experience?
  The dawn of the fintech industry in India has simplified financial services and made it fairly straightforward and accessible for an average, smartphone wielding Indian. It has also pushed banks to go digital and keep up with their fast evolving, tech savvy customers. As is the case in many other sectors, breakthrough technologies like AI, Blockchain and IoT have made their mark in the fintech industry as well. An example worth mentioning is that of one of the oldest banks in our country – SBI. SBI Mutual Funds was reported to have deployed chatbots to effectively reach millions of their customers. Also now instead of having to rely on human judgement, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning help a financial institution to evaluate a customer’s creditworthiness. These technological solutions make things more user friendly. It goes to prove that customer experience and satisfaction has never been more paramount in the financial sector than at present, especially given the wide variety of options for customers.  
  1. Please talk about the operational and financial benefits Fintech solutions offered to SMB and enterprise customers?
Fintechs have raised substantial amounts of equity and generated a huge interest over the last few years. The tech part of Fintech has been keeping up with continued improving access to data online, such as GST, KYC and variety of bureau scores while simultaneously implementing technology like AI and ML. GST, in particular, has presented a paradigm shift. It offers transparent and reliable business information on a real time basis which neutralizes the scale disadvantage. Fintechs also understand and speak the language of a nascent and rapidly evolving industry enabling them to create disruptive business models of making credit available to MSMEs.   Globally, the current trend is “Neo-banks”. Neo-banks are defined as 100 percent digital banks offering services from accounts, credits and payments without a physical network. However, here at home, regulations do not permit 100 percent digital banks. What would work better is a Fintech-Bank alliance which can do wonders to help improve access and cost of capital for MSMEs.
  1. Payments have been at the forefront of India’s Fintech revolution with UPI, mobile wallets, mobile banking growing aggressively. What are the emerging trends in the digital payments segment in India?
UPI has been a success story and game changer for every industry. The latest Worldline report titled "India Digital Payments Report - Q3 2019" reported that the total volume of UPI transactions in Q3 2019 in India touched 2.7 billion - a whopping 183 % increase from the same in the July-September quarter, a year ago. In terms of value, UPI clocked Rs 4.6 trillion, up 189 % from Q3 2018. It is very visible that UPI payments have now become a way of life. Initially, it was only Gen Z that had embraced this trend but nowadays, even the local coconut seller or paan shopkeeper have QR codes from at least 3-4 payment solutions. The coming decade will see wider penetration of digital payments into Tier 3 and Tier 4 markets, reaching over 250 million Indians who are on the Internet but not using digital payments yet.  
  1. Alternative lending is another space driving the Fintech story in India. What are the emerging business models and trends in the alternative lending segment?
Like digital payments, digital EMIs are also becoming increasingly popular in the fintech space. Earlier it would have taken almost 2-3 weeks to sanction a personal loan. This process has now been simplified and is quick and practically paperless and can be completed in five minutes. EMIs are also easily accessible and no longer require a credit card. Just at the beginning of the last decade, this was far from reality.  
  1. InsuranceTech and WealthTech are also finding great acceptance with the growing Fintech space. What are the emerging trends in these segments?
It is exciting to see how InsuranceTech and WealthTech have emerged as hot, new upcoming industries in the last decade. In WealthTech, a prominent service being offered is the consolidation of wealth on a single screen. Platforms like Wealthy are using data aggregation that helps our customers to aggregate their entire wealth at one place. At Wealthy, this feature is also useful for our Wealth Managers as they are empowered to help their clients make better, informed choices. The trend in the InsuranceTech industry to look out for is customisable policies. For example, customers can now look at getting an insurance for a one-time illness like dengue or perhaps even for small hospitalization expenses.
  1. With the boom in digital transactions, the security of customers’ payment data has become extremely crucial. How are we securing the digital transactions and customers’ data?
There are no laws on preventing the misuse of personal data, although the Supreme Court defended that the right to privacy is every Indian’s fundamental right. However, localisation of data along with the recently proposed Data Protection Bill will go a long way in ensuring the security of customers’ data. Many fintech platforms are taking measures to ensure that their customer data is secure. At Wealthy we value our customers and have taken stringent measures to ensure we don’t leave any room for data breach. Currently we have opted for bank-grade security features and we are building teams to take care of data protection.  
  1. What are the challenges that exist in the Fintech space in India?
A major challenge in the Fintech space is bridging the trust gap. In the wake of the economic slowdown and recent incidents of collapsing financial institutions, building and maintaining trust is crucial for any fintech company. We can see that the market is adopting new technology and services as there is a huge need for convenience. However, there is still the underlying issue of trust. This is true especially in the Personal Wealth Management space. The approach we have taken for this is to use a hybrid approach of an online platform, coupled with the human touch of our Wealth Managers who offer personalised advice and counsel when it comes to making investments.  
  1. What are the future opportunities you see in the Fintech space in India?
We have witnessed a great shift from offline to online in the past decade. Digitisation and technology have taken over every area of our life and has redefined it in a way that was almost unimaginable, just 10 years ago. The average Indian’s relationship with money has changed drastically - from swiping cards to scanning QR codes, saving tax with just three clicks and making investment decisions by filling just a basic KYC. That said, there is still a huge need to bring these advancements to over 40% of the population of our country. Financial inclusion of the rural population is a big opportunity we have yet to explore. We will need newer products and services to cater to the needs of the people who are currently under-served by our banking system. That is a big opportunity and the current industry offerings just barely scratch the surface.

Title: SBIFunds Management Private Limitedbecomes the first AMC  to adopt Stewardship Code in India
Content:
• Stewardship Code implemented before SEBI deadline of April 1, 2020
SBI Funds Management Private Limited (SBIFMPL), a joint venture between State Bank of India (“SBI”), India’s largest bank, and Amundi, Europe’s largest asset manager has adopted Stewardship Code ahead of SEBI mandateeffective from April 1, 2020.  In doing this, theyhave become the first fund house to implementthe Stewardship Code in India. The AMC had already adopted a Responsible Investment Policy, and the Stewardship Code is a natural extension to its commitment to become the most respected and trusted asset manager in the country. SBI Mutual Fund has been a pioneer in ESG investing in India. The Stewardship Code, which they now haveadopted highlights the stewardship responsibilities undertaken by the fund house to actively monitor, engage with and intervene, if needed, in the companies under its coverage. Ashwani Bhatia MD & CEO, SBIFMPL said,“We have a highly committed investment team who follow robust systems and processes in the investor’s interest. The Stewardship Code shall guide SBIFMPL’s vision to be a trusted and respected Asset Manager by being an ethical, responsive and innovative partner in investment solutions. SBI Mutual Fund is also the lead investor in the climate change engagement and has been ahead of its peers in adopting best practices.” According to Navneet Munot, ED & CIO, SBIFMPL,“We have a fiduciary duty to create long term value for all our stakeholders. The Stewardship Code gives an insight into the AMC’s strong ESG integration initiatives and firm resolve to take decisions in the best interest of its unit holders.” “SBI Mutual Fund was the first mutual fund in India to adopt the CFA Institute’s Asset Manager Code of Conduct, is the signatory of UN-supported Principles of Responsible Investing and claims compliance with the Global Investment PerformanceStandards (GIPS®). The AMC shall continue to monitor and engage constructively with its investee companies on matters related to Environmental footprint, social impact and Governance.” adds Navneet. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has mandated all Mutual Funds and AIFs in the country to adopt a Stewardship Code, which is applicable for investments in listed equities. The Code will come into effect from the financial year beginning April 01, 2020. By adopting this Code, SBI Mutual Fund continues to demonstrate leadership and readiness towards an evolving responsible investment ecosystem within the country. Title: Providing Solace to the Unbanked
Content: Sumeet Puri, Senior VP and Global Head of Field Technology, Solace talks about the evolution of computing and data requirements for financial institutions and recommends how they can reach out faster and real time to more of the unbanked.  How event-driven thinking facilitates the data movement needs of financial institutions in India? If you look at the historical context on which our applications were built, we have computer as one of the most batch made systems. We used to do computing within ourselves using batch pace and then that gradually evolved into computing style, remote computer communication style interactions and then fast forward to more recent times from service oriented architectures to APIs. All of these different phases of evolution were taking steps of being real-time as volume is growing and response time is further shortening. I think for the current wave of working real-time requirement is very tough especially for financial institutions. We have looked at how NPCI in India is making payments happen in real-time. Risk, fraud etc all these calculations are done very quickly in real time, and so to achieve this in an agile manner, things had to get evolved holistically. If you have seen the lifecycle of somebody it's a series of events, and if you triggered a payment that's an event. It goes through validation, funding, risk, checks, all of these steps. Each one of these is an event. So, credit initiation, credit approval, these are also events. So what if the business was not orchestrated by two or more events but events floating in an out in a process called the event mesh. Your business analysis, micro funding services, they are just consumed by us as filtered events. You could roll out the micro services faster, they could just wire tap the events and let them flow through the mesh in a quicker manner, do their piece and then public can see that there's a dual events back. So, to see that the application which can be much more responsive and deal in a much bigger scale. From an event mesh perspective you will be able to go, from all of the magnitude, higher scale and then you can introduce machine learning very quickly and also do a cloud based systems better. So, that's the whole system of event mesh. We at Solace, we provide this infrastructure, we provide a series of event brokers that can network you further, you can run them in the cloud and create this distributed event mesh so that your micro services, APIs, applications, even IoT devices can just publish and subscribe, can just generate and consume these events for a much more real-time and higher velocity in a platform especially at India's scale. What are the challenges that traditional banks face in modernizing their banking systems and how do they overcome them? If you look at it from the global perspective, a lot of banking which started branch based or bank server based especially in the core banking structure, they had a lot of mainframe structures. Mainframes are known for what they do at a number of countries, but then open systems were built around them. In India, most of the banks, because we started later in the digital adoption journey, have a lot of open systems back here. But still a lot of systems which worked well in the past face challenges in this current age of smart-phones with all the traffic through the roof which is fantastic. If you look at the number of customers which have been brought into financial inclusions with bank accounts all of these are basically digital publishers and subscribers. They are a part of the digital economy. So banks have to achieve this digital scale. But the technology used in the past years was not built for that. It was built for the electronic colour probably internet banking at the best. So, now to deal with this scale, we need better newer faster products and to serve the durability faster, so agility from that perspective, I think we have to relook at our infrastructure. So, the banks and traditional economic institutions need to rethink their current technology and culture working as a wall towards a more modern real-time thinking also put capabilities around their existing system. They should also draw lines to say that from here onwards newer system would be built with the more real-time event streaming paradigm, while opportunistically the existing systems could be upgraded by adapters and other tools and mechanisms that are required. Our recommendation is, you lay out a foundation, put an event mesh there start on boarding events, use the micro services and also the cloud based paradigms and then you gradually transform because a big bang never really works. How financial institutions in India can achieve hyper-connectivity and reach out to the under banked? The good news is that as part of policies under banked are being reached anyways. So, from the outreach to the villages to even the unbanked areas in cities to those hiding in front of our eyes you need an infrastructure of scales to the next level. The cost on action has to be significantly reduced because the under banked and unbanked sectors cannot afford those high costs, be it the cost of account opening or the cost of a payment or a KYC etc. So, your infrastructure has to scale to a certain level, so that you can drive this cost n down so from our perspective. Solace has got customers in India such as Airtel, Reliance Jio, the National Stock Exchange as well so all of these organisations that are known for scale. We sit behind Airtel's prepaid network for example, as well as Jio's. So every time you top-up your phone, we are the underlined infrastructure that takes that to various billing systems and too up systems. We achieve all of these end to end in less than 5 seconds for 97%-98% of the transactions. Applying that same real-time behaviour to the banking sector, we can actually use this mobility capability and go into the unbanked sectors. So with mobile banking or even assisted mobiles or maybe a village leader has the digital platform and people out there interact till they become digitally self sufficient. the need is the ability to carry these events in real-time, end to end in a low latency manner—sub second, submili second kind of latency. I think once you have that scale it could provide maybe 25 million messages per second. Achieving that scale on a structure allows you to grow around it at a much reduced cost per interaction and that's how you go into India's scale

Title: RBI’s Directions concerning the cryptocurrency transactions are being awaited
Content:
The banking ban on cryptocurrencies trade got lifted by the Supreme Court on Mach 4<sup>th</sup> post which the stakeholders are looking for clear directives from the RBI to banks to allowance on transactions in cryptocurrencies.

According to a report a law firm representing cryptocurrency traders, Fintech Lawyers has reportedly written to the government as well as the RBI for the directions. Mohammad Danish of Fintech Lawyers said in a letter to the finance secretary and the RBI that in most of such cases the bank have not been informing its customers via any sort of written communication but the customers have been verbally informed that they are awaiting RBI’s notification in this regard.

According to the bankers’ statement despite SC ruling, the legality of crypto-trade is not clearly defined in India which is the reason why the platforms for crypto-trade would be opened only on explicit regulatory orders from either the parliament or the central bank. Further it said that the domestic banks as well as their capabilities would be tested in regards with allowing such trades without a sound supervisory mechanism which governs cryptocurrencies.

The resistance is evident despite Supreme Court order from March 4 which lifted the banking ban on cryptocurrency trading in the India. In April 2018, The RBI has virtually banned cryptocurrency trading in the country. Circulars cautioning users, holders and traders of virtual currencies, including Bitcoin also got issued by the RBI.

RBI is however said to be looking forward to file a review petition in SC to hold back cryptocurrency transactions in India. RBI is of course also concerned about the drawbacks which would come along with cryptocurrency transactions. Nevertheless, the central bank thinks that allowing cryptocurrency transactions has higher probability of putting the banking system at risk.

The SC in its order reportedly said that citizens have the right to create new industry of cryptocurrency and they also have the fundamental right to trade. The SC has moreover said that the right to create something new which won’t violate any of our existing provision is undoubtedly an unsaid fundamental law.

The apex court stated that the RBI couldn’t successfully show that how cryptocurrencies can put the banking systems at risk. Simultaneously the court found out that the banking system has been a lifeline for virtual currency exchanges. But no announcements from the government or the RBI since then is a concern at present.

Title: “Tonetag is not competitor of payment companies but their technology” enabler
Content: Sudeshna Singh, Head—Marketing & Communications, Tonetag outlines her solutions, elaborates on the challenges and explains her competition. What is the underlying principle behind your technology? Tonetag is basically a technology. It uses sound as a technology to enable multiple use cases. Sound is a most important element through which the universe communicates with us. You would agree with me that since our existence sound has enabled a very seamless channel of communication between the most complicated machine known to mankind, which is a human body. And right now this conversation is happening because sound is playing a very important role. What are the solutions Tonetag is offering? Tonetag is using this existing power of sound and harnessing it to enable device to device and human to device interaction enabling data transfer and creating a very seamless and secure channel of communication between the devices. The company has built use cases specifically in payment which is a very important industry for us and retail in terms of customer engagement. So we have multiple use cases in Payment and retail engagement. In payments, we work with banks where we give our technology as a SDK which any of the payment companies can take, integrate it into their applications, and they are good to go to enable sound based payments for their customers. What were the challenges and how are you looking to overcome them? When we initially started, that time digital payment was still very new in India and people were not very secure with using their phone to make digital payments. So the challenges we faced initially were in educating the entire ecosystem and then slowly when we started getting partners like lots of banks. Then people started saying that this is a secure technology. The experience is faster than paying by card or more secure than making a QR code payment. Who are your competitors in this space?  When we talk about competition, we have to remember we are a technology enabler and we create technology, and give it to partners and they intake it. As competition I would say there are companies globally, who are using sound as a technology to transfer data, like data can be an audio file or a content, but nobody is using sound as a technology to enable payments the way we are doing. The kind of measures which we have taken to build as security, and how fast we are processing the information is unique and hence we have filed 15 patents on these. I would say, there is no competition as such but the market perceived payment companies as  our competitors but they are not our competitorsbut rather can be our partners. We are not competition to any payment companies but a technology enabler for them.
